answer.answer:
Delivering prefabricated timber facade panels that do not repeat rests on four upstream requirements, and none of them is a machine: early contractor involvement, DfMA for the fabrication process, an integrated supply chain, and precise up-front planning, the last of these by far the most widely drawn on in the coded record. The non-repeating panels are reached not by abandoning standardisation but through it: a kit-of-parts configurator sits on top of highly standardised components and is what carries mass-customisation, while a fully bespoke design actively constrains modularity, so panel variety has to be bought inside a standardised system rather than outside it. Prefabrication also depends on regulatory and legal compliance, whose cited mechanism is third-party certification and traceability, which is the only path in the material that bears on an envelope performance target. Timber facade work off-site is a mature, deployed practice here, though no energy-performance certification scheme, Minergie included, appears anywhere in the record.

**What prefabrication requires**

Four things run upstream of PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", which 20 of the 50 coded cases draw on:

- CO11 "Early contractor involvement" (Condition) enablesCapability PR2, backed by peer-reviewed evidence. The mechanism is that integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party, manufacturer, fabricator or contractor, to be involved in the early design phase, and a project delivery method that involves participants in early design should be selected. [1] CO11 is drawn on by 14 of the 50 cases; the edge itself is carried by 13.
- PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" (Process) enablesCapability PR2, peer-reviewed, DfMA orienting the project toward offsite manufacture [1]. PR9 is drawn on by 15 cases and the edge is carried by 15.
- VA14 "Integrate supply chain" (Value) enablesCapability PR2, peer-reviewed: supply chain integration supports the offsite production line [1]. VA14 is drawn on by 14 cases, the edge by 12.
- PR2 dependsOn RI14 "Rely on precise planning" (Risk), peer-reviewed, since prefabrication relies on precise up-front planning and logistics [1]. RI14 is drawn on by 36 of the 50 cases, the edge by 18.

The asymmetry matters: RI14 at 36 cases is drawn on nearly three times as often as the three organisational enablers at 14, 15 and 14. And by category these are a Condition, a Process, a Value and a Risk. There is no Resource among the preconditions for prefabrication in this material, so the delivery problem is one of sequencing, contracting and planning discipline, not of acquiring equipment.

CO11 also runs to AT12 "Integrated design-DFAB process" (10 of 50 carry that edge) and to PR9 itself (11 carry), so early involvement is the common root of both the integrated process and the DfMA orientation.

**Non-repeating panels**

The route to panel variety is AT7 "Highly standardised" (Attribute) enablesCapability AR6 "Configurators/kit-of-parts" (Artefact), on standards evidence, where modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components [1], and then AR6 enablesCapability PR11 "Mass-customisation" (Process), peer-reviewed, because the design configurator integrates customisation data into robotic manufacturing [1]. AT7 is drawn on by 25 cases, AR6 by 12, PR11 by 17; the two edges are carried by 11 and 9 cases respectively.

The counter-route is a warning: AT1 "Bespoke/customised design" (Attribute) constrains AT2 "Modular" (Attribute), peer-reviewed, because integral architecture couples functions tightly to components, constraining modular interchange [1]. That edge is carried by only 4 of the 50 cases, but it is the direction of travel to avoid: treating each panel as a one-off rather than as a configured instance. Two risks quantify the cost of getting the balance wrong: RI15 "Design compromise/over standardised" is drawn on by 17 cases and RI19 "Production/assembly restriction" by 25, the latter one of the most common risks in the record.

Note also AT7 enablesCapability VA7 "Reduce construction complexity" (15 of 50 carry it), so the standardised base that makes the configurator possible is also what pays back at assembly.

**The envelope performance target**

Nothing in the context names Minergie or any other energy or envelope certification scheme, and no enabler in the material stands for performance certification. The nearest path is PR2 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" (Risk), peer-reviewed, where a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability [1]. RI18 is drawn on by 12 of the 50 cases and this edge by 10. AR4 "Performance-based design" (Artefact) exists in the record and is drawn on by 6 of 50, but it carries no dependency edges, so there is no asserted path from it to prefabrication or to the facade. Treat the certification requirement as an inference from the offsite compliance edge, not as a documented Minergie path.

**Deployed evidence**

Off-site timber fabrication at full maturity is well attested. Process RP6 performs assembly and timber joinery cutting, works on the structural core, is deployed off-site and sits at technology readiness level 9 [2], as do RP3, adopted to address quality, integration and market [3] and RP7, adopted to address digital and market [4]. Those three work on the structural core rather than the facade. The closest record to the question is census_RXH10-2: adopted to address market, performing assembly and timber joinery cutting, working on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, at technology readiness level 9 [5], and it uses timber. For an off-site facade process specifically, RP8 performs inspection and material handling on the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, deployed off-site, at technology readiness level 9 [6], though the context does not give its material. The one timber record here with a named firm is census_RXT1-2: developed by Firm_128, using timber [7], but the context gives no process profile for it.

Two limits on that evidence. The context does not link any of these deployed cases to the enablers discussed above, so the case-level picture of which requirements each one met is not in front of me; the counts quoted come from the coded record of 50 cases. And no record here combines timber, a facade and non-repeating panels in one deployment, so the mass-customisation route via the configurator is supported by literature and by the coded counts rather than by a single matching deployed facade case.
